transcript:
User: Yeah I saw your thing online. Honestly this smells like one of those AI scam gadgets. Convince me it's not garbage.
Agent: Totally fair reaction — a lot of stuff out there is garbage.  

Before I try to convince you of anything, what kind of business are you running and where do missed calls or lost leads show up for you right now?
User: Ortiz Roofing, Dallas. Miss about 30 calls a week during jobs. Feels like money slipping through my fingers.
Agent: Got it, Ortiz Roofing in Dallas — and yeah, “money slipping through my fingers” makes sense if you’re missing 30 calls a week while you’re on roofs.  

When those calls come in and you can’t grab the phone, what actually happens — do they hit voicemail, an answering service, or do they just ring out and disappear?
User: They usually just ring out and disappear. I'm too busy to deal with voicemails during jobs.
Agent: Yeah, that “ring out and disappear” is exactly where the money slips away.  

If even a third of those 30 calls a week are real roofing jobs, what do you figure each one is worth to you on average?
User: Average job brings in $1,800. But how do I know you're not some robot just repeating that back to me?
Agent: Makes sense, $1,800 a job means even a handful of those “disappearing” calls is real money.  

On the robot thing — I’m software, yeah, but my whole job is to listen, use your actual numbers, and help you decide if stopping those missed-call losses is worth it to you; do you care more about *how* it works or *whether* it pencils out first?
User: Alright, I'll bite. So, who sees my data? Is this some robot calling my customers?
Agent: Good question — you should be picky about this stuff.  

Two parts: 1) your call data stays between you, our system, and Jay’s small tech team that sets you up, and 2) yes, when you miss a call, it’s a very natural-sounding automated agent that answers in your name, grabs the details, and can even book the estimate instead of letting it just ring out.  

What worries you more — someone “robot-y” talking to your customers, or where the call recordings and info are stored?
User: Both, honestly. How do I know this isn't recorded and stored somewhere sketchy? Prove it's secure.
Agent: Totally hear you — if it isn’t secure, it isn’t worth it.  

So, concrete stuff: we use encrypted connections end‑to‑end (same standard banks use), data lives in reputable US/EU cloud providers with strict access controls, and only your account + Jay’s small technical team can see your call info, not random third parties or ad networks.  

If we walked through this on a quick live call with Jay, would you want to drill into *where* data is stored and who can access it, or *how long* it’s kept and what can be deleted?
User: Alright, fair enough. Let’s see if this live call with Jay can clear up where my data actually goes.
Agent: Got it, that’s exactly what Jay’s best at walking through.  

Before you two talk, can I grab one more thing from you so we can ballpark how much those 30 missed calls a week might actually be costing you—roughly what percentage of people who reach you end up booking a job, maybe half, 60%?
User: I’d estimate about 40% of those missed calls would book. Go on, I'm curious about this math.
Agent: Perfect, thanks for giving me a real number.  

So with your 30 missed calls a week, 40% of those turning into $1,800 jobs—that’s about $21,600 just walking away every week when calls ring out and disappear.  

Hearing it that way, does that feel high, low, or kind of uncomfortably accurate for what slips through at Ortiz Roofing right now?
User: Uncomfortably accurate, but still not convinced. How do I stay in control of this "live call" thing?
Agent: Yeah, that “uncomfortably accurate” feeling is usually the right one.  

So, the live call is just a 20‑minute walkthrough — you see exactly how it works, what control you have over scripts, data, and when it picks up, and if it feels off, you walk away; for that, is later this week or sooner this week better for you?
User: Alright, I’ll bite. Let’s go for later this week. How do I set this up?
Agent: Nice, let’s do it.  

First thing I need is your first name, and I’ll take it slow on the spelling.
User: Alright, it's Sam. S-A-M. Let's see if this live call is worth my time.
User: Mm-hmm.
Agent: Thanks, Sam.  

Quick check — you’re in Dallas, so you’re on Central time, right?
User: Yeah, that's right. Dallas, Central time. Just don't go calling my customers without me knowing, got it?
Agent: Got it, we don’t touch your customers without you knowing exactly how and when.  

For the call with Jay to walk through all that control, would you rather do Thursday or Friday this week?
User: Alright, pencil me in for Thursday. But mark my words, I'm still skeptical.
Agent: Totally fine to stay skeptical, Sam — you’re just committing to 20 minutes, not your firstborn.  

On Thursday I can get you in as soon as 10:00 or 10:45 Central; which one works better for you?
User: Alright, let’s do 10:45 Central. But remember, I'm watching every step of this.
Agent: One moment while I confirm that for you.
Agent: You’re all set, Sam — you and Jay are booked for Thursday at 10:45 Central. You’ll get a text with the confirmation and a link, so you can add it to your calendar or reschedule if you need to. Really glad you called in and pushed on this; Jay’s expecting your skepticism and will walk you through exactly how and when it touches your customers. Have a great rest of your day — we’ll talk Thursday.
